The Hameln-Bodenwerder circle is left out, matching the duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg keyframe of 1643.

ledger.note: 15 August 1235: Conrad II reaches 'the official acknowledgement of Hildesheim as a Prince-bishopric' at the Mainz Reichstag (infobox 'Imperial immediacy: 1235'); Louis the Pious had founded the bishopric in 815.

1519: the Hildesheim Diocesan Feud. The conflict 'broke out in 1519'; Prince-Bishop John IV with the town of Hildesheim, Henry the Middle of Lüneburg and the counts of Schaumburg, Diepholz and Hoya beat the Welf principalities of Wolfenbüttel and Calenberg at Soltau on 28 June 1519.
13 May 1523: the Quedlinburg Recess ends the feud, the 'last medieval feud'.

13 May 1523: the Great Stift is lost. 'Hildesheim was left with 4 of its 22 Ämter, plus the towns of Hildesheim and Peine, and the Kleines Stift'; Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel 'gained many Ämter, abbeys, and towns', Calenberg 'fortified seats, Ämter, towns including Dassel and Bodenwerder, half of Hameln'. Hildesheim 'had won militarily, but lost politically'. The extent is the researcher's reading; Peine stayed with Hildesheim.

region.text: the Great Stift and the Hameln-Bodenwerder seats

ledger.note: 1573: the Wittelsbach bishops. 'Its bishops were members of the powerful House of Wittelsbach from 1573 until 1761' (Ernest was bishop 1573-1612, Ferdinand administrator 1612-1650; Clemens August was also Archbishop of Cologne). Same state, new dynasty.

1643: the restitution. 'During the restitution in 1643' the bishopric recovered 'large parts of the lost estates', while the offices Aerzen, Grohnde and Lutter am Barenberge 'remained with Calenberg and Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel' (the feud page calls it 'the Main Treaty of Hildesheim returned most of the lost territories').
1803: 'during the German Mediatisation, Hildesheim was secularised and its territory was annexed to Prussia.' The page does not mention a 1802 Prussian occupation and gives no month.

wars.name: Hildesheim Diocesan Feud
wars.outcome: Hildesheim won at Soltau on 28 June 1519 but the Quedlinburg Recess of 13 May 1523 left it 4 of its 22 Ämter, the towns of Hildesheim and Peine and the Kleines Stift; the restitution of 1643 returned most of the rest.

Aerzen, Grohnde and Lutter stayed outside; the rest is the researcher's reading.
